introduction: These passages, most from talks and letters of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, speak frankly and often severely of the East of his day: a faith's first purity forgotten, rulers without vision, women shut away, a people asleep to their own decline, and Persia, once a light of the world, in ruins; and beside this, the hope of renewal and the claim that East and West each need what the other has. Some sentences describe whole peoples, Arabs, Copts and nomads among them, in terms a reader today will not accept as they stand. Each of the forty-eight quotations is read here beside one from elsewhere. Most stand alongside, many of them prophets rebuking their own people, as these passages do: Isaiah, Lamentations, Jesus over Jerusalem, Khayyam on Persia's ruins, Tagore's prayer for his country. Ten push back or add a side, more than usual: Montaigne on who is called barbarous, the mote and the beam, Paul's 'of one blood', Macaulay and Kipling as the Western contempt of the time, Paul on women's silence as the West's own inheritance, Gandhi, Okakura and Montesquieu's Persian looking back at Europe.
questions: Most of these criticisms are made by an Easterner of his own world, as the prophets rebuked their own people. What difference does it make who is speaking, and to whom?
Some passages describe whole peoples harshly. How do you read them now, and what in the rest of the collection corrects them?

The readings say that the East should take material civilization from the West, and the West spiritual civilization from the East. Gandhi and Okakura would put it differently. What does each region have that the other needs?
Several readings trace the East's decline to the seclusion of women. Paul's 'let your women keep silence' was long obeyed in the West. Whose failing was it?
One reading says that Persians, hungry, believe themselves satisfied, while Americans, satisfied, hunger. Which is the more dangerous condition?

outside.why: The Revelation tells a church that it has a name that it lives, and is dead, and bids it remember how it received and heard.
Mary Wollstonecraft wrote in 1792: strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, and there will be an end to blind obedience.
Kipling's ballad says that East is East and West is West, and yet that there is neither when two strong men stand face to face.

Okakura wrote for Western readers of a Japanese way founded on the adoration of the beautiful among the sordid facts of everyday existence. Besides religion, what has the East to give that the West lacks?
Isaiah says that the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light.
Proverbs says that righteousness exalteth a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people.
The Qur'an says that God changeth not the condition of a folk until they first change that which is in their hearts.
A Persian poet, in FitzGerald's English, says that the lion and the lizard keep the courts where Jamshyd gloried and drank deep.
Lamentations begins: how doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people; she that was great among the nations.
Paul's letter asks that prayers be made for kings, and for all that are in authority.
Isaiah says that they shall build the old wastes, and repair the desolations of many generations.
Isaiah says of his own country that truth is fallen in the street, and equity cannot enter.
Jesus says that every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation, and every house divided shall not stand.
Plato held that cities will have no rest from their evils until philosophers are kings.
The Preacher says: woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child, and thy princes eat in the morning.
Isaiah says of his own people's leaders that the watchmen are blind, sleeping, loving to slumber.
Thucydides has the Athenians say that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.
Paul writes that it is high time to awake out of sleep, for the night is far spent.
Isaiah complains of his own people that the ox knoweth his owner, but they do not consider.
Matthew tells of wise men who came from the east, having seen a star.

Macaulay, deciding how India should be taught, claimed that a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia. How does the consul's opinion in this story sound beside that, and what did the reply to him rest on?
Jesus says of the teachers of his own people: laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men.
Jesus says that unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.

Montaigne, hearing of peoples newly met, found nothing barbarous in them, except that every one gives the title of barbarism to everything that is not in use in his own country. How should a harsh word about a whole people, spoken in a letter, be read today?
Mark Twain wrote that travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness. The charge here is that a people prefer no others to themselves. Of which peoples is that not true?
Jesus asks why you behold the mote in your brother's eye, and consider not the beam in your own. When is it right to speak of another people's faults, and who may?
Paul told the Athenians that God hath made of one blood all nations of men. What in the rest of these readings corrects the description of nomads as living an animalistic life?
In the parable a man with full barns says to his soul: take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry.
The last psalm says: praise him with the sound of the trumpet, with the timbrel and dance, with stringed instruments and organs.
Tennyson wrote that the woman's cause is man's: they rise or sink together, dwarfed or godlike, bond or free.
Paul's letter says: let your women keep silence in the churches, for it is not permitted unto them to speak. Was the low estate of women a failing of the East?
The women at Seneca Falls in 1848 had still to declare that all men and women are created equal.
The Qur'an addresses men who believe and women who believe, men who speak the truth and women who speak the truth, side by side.
Shelley's traveller finds the boast of a king of kings on a pedestal, and round it the lone and level sands.
Goethe remarked that a man who has no acquaintance with foreign languages knows nothing of his own.
The Revelation addresses a church that says, I am rich and have need of nothing, and knows not that it is poor.
Ezekiel sees the glory of the God of Israel come from the way of the east.
Jesus asks what it shall profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul.
Montesquieu imagined a Persian in Paris writing home that the French never walk: they run, they fly. What does each side see of the other that it cannot see of itself?
Kipling urged the West to take up the White Man's burden and serve its captives' need. That is the view of the East this reading says has been overturned. What had to be shown, and to whom?
John the Baptist says that the axe is laid unto the root of the trees.
Jesus says to the people of his own town: verily I say unto you, no prophet is accepted in his own country.
Gandhi judged Western civilization to be such that one has only to be patient and it will be self-destroyed. Who has taken what from whom, and what should the East not want back?
Jesus laments over his own city: thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee.
John's Gospel says: he came unto his own, and his own received him not.
The psalm says: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
Tagore prayed for a country where the mind is without fear and the world is not broken up by narrow domestic walls.
The Song of Solomon sings that the winter is past, and the time of the singing of birds is come.
